title: Acute Pancreatitis
scenario: A 47-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe, steady epigastric pain radiating to the back that began after a weekend of heavy alcohol use. He reports nausea, several episodes of vomiting, and that the pain worsens when lying flat.

lines: 47-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, rated 9/10, onset this morning after weekend alcohol binge. Nauseated with three episodes of vomiting. Guarding of the abdomen with diffuse epigastric tenderness. Appears diaphoretic and restless. Alert and oriented x3.
Two large-bore IV lines established. Labs, lipase, amylase, and CBC drawn. Abdominal ultrasound and CT ordered. Client made NPO. Cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry applied.
IV lactated Ringer's bolus infusing per order. IV opioid analgesia administered for pain. Antiemetic given. Nasogastric tube considered pending provider assessment.
Reports pain now 3/10. Less restless, no further vomiting. Urine output improving. Vital signs trending toward normal. Tolerating small sips of ice chips without nausea.
Reports drinking 6-8 beers daily, more on weekends
Two prior ED visits for abdominal pain
Lactated Ringer's IV bolus, then maintenance infusion; titrate to urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/hr
IV opioid analgesia for pain per protocol
IV antiemetic as needed for nausea
Notify provider for SpO2 < 92% or urine output < 30 mL/hr

children.subject: Medical-Surgical

options.text: Epigastric pain radiating to the back rated 9/10

children.rationale: Severe pain, hypotension with tachycardia, a markedly elevated lipase, and persistent vomiting all point to acute pancreatitis with early fluid loss and require prompt intervention. Normal orientation and no allergies are reassuring, not concerning.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it indicates the inflammatory process, developing fluid volume deficit, or both. Each finding may indicate more than one.
children.rationale: Elevated lipase and leukocytosis reflect pancreatic inflammation. Hypotension and vomiting with low output reflect third-spacing and fluid loss. Tachycardia is a compensatory response driven by both inflammation and hypovolemia.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Complete the sentence. The nurse determines that the priority problem is {1}, and the first intervention should be {2}.
children.rationale: The immediate threat in acute pancreatitis is deficient fluid volume from third-spacing and vomiting; aggressive IV isotonic fluid resuscitation is the priority intervention to restore perfusion. Oral fluids are contraindicated while NPO.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.

rows.text: Provide a high-fat meal to maintain calories
Administer IV analgesia for pain control
Encourage the client to lie flat and supine

children.rationale: Resting the pancreas with NPO, isotonic IV fluids, and pain control are standard care. A high-fat meal stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and worsens inflammation, and lying flat increases pain; both are contraindicated.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: After starting IV fluid resuscitation and analgesia, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Encourage a full oral diet immediately

children.rationale: Monitoring output, calcium (which drops in pancreatitis), and pain response, while maintaining NPO, are appropriate actions. Advancing the diet prematurely and stopping monitoring would be unsafe.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Which findings indicate the treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.
children.rationale: Reduced pain, a normalizing blood pressure and heart rate, and improving urine output all show that fluid resuscitation and pain management are working. Ongoing vomiting would indicate a lack of improvement.
